- When sentiment is consistently bullish (≥0.67) and model forecasts rise steadily, cap the upward slope to avoid overshoot after recent spikes.
- If supply net is heavily negative (e.g., -14.98 or lower) and true prices dip sharply, adjust forecast downward by 5–10% to account for policy-driven volatility.
- After a strong upward spike (e.g., >75), model should not continue rising; introduce mean reversion bias toward prior 5–7 day average.
- When bullish sentiment is low (≤0.33) and supply net is negative, forecast should not be overly optimistic — reduce slope by 10–20% to reflect bearish sentiment.
- If model forecasts are flat or rising slowly but true prices show sharp declines (e.g., >10% drop from peak), introduce downward bias starting 3–5 days after peak.
- For 30-day forecasts with high event count and negative supply net, reduce forecast mean by 3–5% to reflect over-supply pressure.
- If sentiment history shows alternating bullish/bearish cycles, model should not overfit to recent trend — use 3–5 day moving average to smooth out sentiment-driven noise.
